gloss_terse: Nod — the land east of Eden where Cain wandered as a fugitive after killing Abel
gloss_readable: Nod appears only once in Scripture, naming the region where Cain settled after murdering his brother. The Hebrew root suggests wandering or exile, making this a fitting designation for the fugitive's new home. Genesis describes it as east of Eden, a geographical marker that also carries theological weight—movement away from God's presence into a land defined by restlessness.

senses.1: The proper name of a territory mentioned in Genesis 4:16, literally 'the land of Nod,' where Cain dwelt after being banished. The name itself resonates with the verb for wandering (נוד), creating a wordplay: the wanderer goes to the land of Wandering. Ancient versions struggled with whether to treat this as a place name or translate it descriptively as 'land of fugitives.'

gloss_terse: Nodab — an Arab tribe defeated by the Transjordanian Israelite tribes, mentioned alongside Jetur and Naphish
gloss_readable: Nodab appears in a brief catalogue of nomadic peoples conquered by the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh. Chronicles links them with descendants of Ishmael, placing them within the broader Arabian tribal network that Israel encountered east of the Jordan. The name's etymology remains uncertain, though some connect it to the root for nobility or willing offering.

senses.1: A gentile designation (people group name) found in 1 Chronicles 5:19, identifying one of three Arab tribes defeated by Israelite forces. The context pairs Nodab with Jetur and Naphish, both attested elsewhere as Ishmaelite clans, suggesting a similar origin. The conjunction prefix in Hebrew ('and-Nodab') shows this is part of a military victory list.

gloss_terse: beautify, glorify, adorn with praise — to honor God through worship and exaltation
gloss_readable: This rare verb appears in Moses' victory song at the Red Sea, where Israel responds to divine deliverance with worship. The root connects to beauty and comeliness, suggesting that true praise adorns its object. The parallel with 'exalt' indicates this is no mere aesthetic appreciation but active glorification through word and deed. Later Jewish tradition developed this root further in the language of beautifying commandments.

senses.1: The Hiphil form (causative) meaning 'I will beautify/adorn him,' used in Exodus 15:2 with God as the direct object. Moses declares his intent to glorify YHWH through praise, paralleled by 'I will exalt him.' The verb's aesthetic roots (related to נָאָה 'comely, beautiful') suggest worship that honors God by presenting him in his true splendor. Ancient versions render this as 'glorify' (Greek δοξάσω, Latin glorificabo), capturing the theological sense.

gloss_terse: abide, dwell, remain — to settle or remain in a place (denominative from 'dwelling')
gloss_readable: This verb appears once in Habakkuk's description of the arrogant man whose appetite is insatiable. The text says such a person 'will not abide'—cannot find rest or contentment. The verb derives from the noun for dwelling or pasture, creating a verbal form that means to settle down or remain. The textual tradition shows uncertainty here, with various ancient scholars proposing alternative readings.

senses.1: The Qal imperfect 'he will not abide' in Habakkuk 2:5, describing the restless nature of the proud and greedy. Formed from the noun נָוֶה (dwelling, pasture), this denominative verb conveys inability to settle or find rest. The context contrasts with the righteous who live by faithfulness. Some ancient interpreters proposed emendations (the Syriac read 'be at rest,' others suggested 'be satisfied'), reflecting the difficulty of this rare verbal form.

gloss_terse: she who stays at home, dwelling at home — describing women who remain in the household
gloss_readable: This unusual form appears in Psalm 68, a victory hymn celebrating God's triumph and the distribution of spoils. The phrase describes women who remained at home while men went to battle, a common ancient pattern. The construct form links dwelling and house, creating a participial phrase that became proverbial for the homefront.

senses.1: An adjectival participle in construct form, literally 'dwelling of house' or 'the one abiding at home,' found in Psalm 68:12. The feminine form refers to women who stayed in the household while warriors went to battle. This became a way to speak of domestic roles in contrast to military campaigns. The construction uses the root נָוָה (dwell, abide) in participial form attached to 'house,' creating a compound designation.

gloss_terse: Nohah — the fourth son of Benjamin in one genealogical tradition
gloss_readable: Nohah appears only in Chronicles' genealogy of Benjamin, listed as the fourth son. This name doesn't appear in Genesis' account of Benjamin's sons, reflecting the textual variations common in biblical genealogies. Different manuscript traditions and ancient versions show variations in the vocalization, suggesting this was a name whose exact pronunciation was uncertain even in antiquity.

senses.1: A personal name designating Benjamin's fourth son according to 1 Chronicles 8:2. The name appears nowhere else in Scripture, and Genesis 46:21 gives a different list of Benjamin's sons without mentioning Nohah. Greek manuscripts vary (Ἰωα, Νωα, Νουαα), showing textual uncertainty. The meaning remains obscure, though the root could relate to rest or quiet.

gloss_terse: shake, quake, tremble — the earth responding in upheaval to divine presence
gloss_readable: This verb appears in a psalm celebrating God's universal kingship, commanding the earth to shake before the enthroned Lord. The root suggests dangling or swaying motion, different from other Hebrew words for trembling. Paired with 'be agitated,' it creates an image of cosmic response to divine majesty. Some scholars have questioned the text, but the manuscript tradition supports this rare verb.

senses.1: The Qal imperfect jussive 'let it shake' in Psalm 99:1, describing the earth's reaction to YHWH's reign. The verb (from a root meaning 'dangle, sway') conveys oscillating or unstable movement, paralleled by רָגַז (quake, be agitated). This is theophanic language—creation itself responds physically to divine presence. Arabic cognates support the sense of suspended swaying motion, though some medieval scholars proposed emendations to more common verbs for 'melt' or 'quake.'

gloss_terse: drowsiness, slumber — the sleepy state associated with laziness and poverty
gloss_readable: Proverbs uses this noun to warn against the economic consequences of excessive sleep. Paired with drunkenness, drowsiness becomes emblematic of self-indulgent neglect that leads to poverty. The term is more specific than general sleep, focusing on the heavy, lethargic state that prevents productive work. It's the physical manifestation of spiritual and moral sluggishness.

senses.1: A feminine noun meaning 'drowsiness, somnolence' found in Proverbs 23:21 within a warning about drunkards and gluttons. The text declares that 'drowsiness will clothe a man with rags,' linking this sleepy indolence to poverty. This is not ordinary sleep but the heavy, unproductive lethargy that characterizes the sluggard. The word intensifies the picture of self-destructive habits that Proverbs repeatedly condemns.

gloss_terse: height, elevation — the exalted position or lofty stature of a place
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Psalm 48's hymn to Zion, describing the holy mountain as 'beautiful in elevation.' The term captures both physical height and the elevated status that comes from divine presence. Later Hebrew developed this root toward 'treetop' or 'branch,' but the biblical usage focuses on topographical prominence. The word celebrates Jerusalem's distinction among cities.

senses.1: A masculine noun meaning 'elevation, height' found in Psalm 48:2, modifying Mount Zion. The phrase 'beautiful in elevation' (יְפֵה נוֹף) praises the mountain's position and prominence. This combines geographical reality (Jerusalem sits on a ridge) with theological significance (the city of God occupies the heights). Post-biblical Hebrew shifted this root toward 'bough, treetop,' and Aramaic used related forms for tree branches.

gloss_terse: flee, wander — to move about as homeless refugees without stable residence
gloss_readable: Lamentations uses this disputed verb to describe the tragic fate of Jerusalem's exiles, who both flee and wander without finding rest. The text is difficult, and ancient interpreters struggled with it—some manuscripts suggest different readings. The context is clear: these are displaced persons, ritually unclean outcasts whom others avoid. Whether the verb primarily means 'fly' or 'wander,' the picture is one of desperate homelessness.

senses.1: The Qal perfect 3rd plural 'they fled/wandered' in Lamentations 4:15, describing exiled Jerusalemites as homeless wanderers whom others refuse to shelter. The Hebrew text is textually uncertain—some scholars prefer reading נָדוּ (from the more common root for 'wander, flee'), and the parallel verb 'they wandered' supports this. The context shows ritually unclean refugees being avoided by all nations, unable to find rest anywhere.

gloss_terse: nurse, suckle — to breastfeed an infant
gloss_readable: This verb appears in the Exodus story when Pharaoh's daughter hires Moses' own mother to nurse him. The Hiphil form (causative) indicates making a child suck or providing nursing. The narrative irony is rich: the Hebrew mother is paid to nurse her own son, who will later deliver Israel from Egypt. The word is textually complex, with various proposed readings, but the sense is clear.

senses.1: The Hiphil (causative) form in Exodus 2:9, 'and she nursed him,' describing Moses' mother nursing her own son at Pharaoh daughter's request. The verb means to cause to suck or to give suck (breastfeed). The text has variant readings in manuscripts (Samaritan has a slightly different form), but all agree on the basic meaning. This continues the theme of God's providential protection of the infant who will become Israel's deliverer.

gloss_terse: be sick, be incurable — to suffer from severe or mortal illness
gloss_readable: This verb appears in Psalm 69, one of the great psalms of individual lament, where the speaker describes overwhelming distress. The text is difficult, with ancient interpreters proposing various readings. The basic sense involves serious illness or incurable wounding, whether literal or metaphorical. The psalm's vivid language of drowning and exhaustion suggests this sickness is more than physical—it's the soul-sickness of one abandoned and mocked.

senses.1: The Qal imperfect 1st singular in Psalm 69:20, likely meaning 'I am sick' or 'I am mortally wounded,' though the Hebrew text is disputed. The context speaks of reproach breaking the heart, and the psalmist looking vainly for comforters. Some manuscripts suggest different word divisions or roots (related to 'incurable' or 'hoping'). Ancient versions varied in their rendering, but the overall sense is severe distress, perhaps unto death.

gloss_terse: sprinkle, startle — to cause to leap or to sprinkle (textually uncertain)
gloss_readable: This verb in Isaiah's Servant Song describes the Servant's impact on many nations. Traditional interpretation reads 'sprinkle' (as in ritual cleansing), connecting this to the Servant's atoning work. Others argue for 'startle' or 'cause to leap' from a root meaning to jump. The passage is notoriously difficult, and ancient versions differ. Whether sprinkling or startling, the image conveys the Servant's transformative effect on the nations.

senses.1: The Hiphil imperfect 'he will sprinkle' in Isaiah 52:15, though the meaning is hotly debated. Traditional reading connects this to ritual sprinkling (purification), with the Servant cleansing many nations. Alternative interpretation sees a root meaning 'leap, spring,' yielding 'he will startle/cause to leap'—nations will recoil in surprise at the exalted Servant. Various textual emendations have been proposed ('make tremble,' 'make many silent'), reflecting the difficulty. The context describes kings shutting their mouths in awe.

gloss_terse: damage, injury — harm or loss, especially financial detriment
gloss_readable: This Aramaic loan-word appears only in Esther, where Haman argues to the king that destroying the Jews would not compensate for the damage (financial loss) to the royal interests. The term comes from Persian administrative vocabulary, fitting Esther's court setting. It indicates measurable harm or loss, whether economic or otherwise. The phrase captures Esther's argument that saving her people actually serves the king's advantage.

senses.1: A masculine noun meaning 'injury, damage, loss' found in Esther 7:4, part of Esther's plea to King Ahasuerus. She argues that if her people were merely being sold into slavery, she wouldn't trouble the king, 'for the adversary is not worthy of the damage to the king'—i.e., the harm to royal interests. This is an Aramaic loanword (related to Biblical Aramaic נְזַק), likely borrowed from Persian administrative terminology. The context is economic/political rather than physical injury.

gloss_terse: Nahbi — the representative from the tribe of Naphtali among the twelve spies sent to scout Canaan
gloss_readable: Nahbi appears only in Numbers' list of the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the Promised Land. As Naphtali's representative, he was among those who brought back the discouraging report that led to Israel's forty-year wilderness wandering. The name may relate to being hidden or to prophetic speech, but its etymology remains uncertain.

senses.1: A personal name identifying the Naphtalite spy in Numbers 13:14 (note: the verse reference is given as 13:4 in the source, but textually this appears at 13:14). He was son of Vophsi and represented his tribe in the reconnaissance mission to Canaan. Like most of his fellow spies (except Joshua and Caleb), he likely participated in the negative report that provoked Israel's unbelief. The name's meaning is unclear, though roots related to 'hiding' or 'prophesying' have been suggested.

gloss_terse: Nehum — a leader who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel
gloss_readable: Nehum appears in Nehemiah's list of returnees, parallel to a name in Ezra's account (Rehum). The name means 'comfort' or 'consolation,' appropriate for those returning from exile to rebuild. Such variations between parallel lists are common in Chronicles-Ezra-Nehemiah literature, reflecting different textual traditions or actual name variants used by the same person.

senses.1: A personal name in Nehemiah 7:7, identifying one of the leaders who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel. The name derives from the root נחם (comfort, console). The parallel list in Ezra 2:2 has רְחוּם (Rehum) instead, suggesting either textual variation or that individuals sometimes bore multiple names. Ancient Greek versions render this as Ναουμ (Naoum), showing the name's continuity into the Second Temple period.

gloss_terse: Nahum — the prophet who authored the oracle against Nineveh
gloss_readable: Nahum's name means 'comfort' or 'consolation,' though his prophecy is hardly comforting—at least not to Nineveh. The book opens by identifying him as 'the Elkoshite,' though the location of Elkosh remains uncertain. His oracle celebrates Nineveh's coming destruction, offering comfort to Judah by announcing judgment on their oppressor. The prophetic book is a masterpiece of Hebrew poetry describing divine vengeance.

senses.1: The personal name of the prophet in Nahum 1:1, introducing the entire book. The name derives from נחם (comfort), and some scholars see this as programmatic—Nahum brings comfort to Judah by announcing Nineveh's fall. Ancient versions consistently render this as Naoum or similar. The prophet's historical setting is likely the late 7th century BC, between Assyria's destruction of Thebes (663 BC, mentioned in 3:8) and Nineveh's fall (612 BC, predicted throughout the book).

gloss_terse: of bronze, made of bronze — describing something with the strength and endurance of bronze
gloss_readable: This adjective appears in Job's complaint about his suffering. He asks rhetorically whether his flesh is bronze—whether he has the superhuman strength to endure endless affliction. Bronze represented durability and strength in the ancient world, used for tools, weapons, and construction. Job's point is clear: he's only human, lacking the metallic resilience to withstand such trials indefinitely.

senses.1: An adjective meaning 'of bronze' in Job 6:12, part of Job's rhetorical questions about his capacity to endure. He asks, 'Is my strength the strength of stones? Is my flesh bronze?' The expected answer is no—Job is flesh and blood, not mineral or metal. Later in Job (40:18), bronze again symbolizes extraordinary strength when describing Behemoth's bones. The adjective form derives from the common noun נְחֹשֶׁת (copper, bronze).

gloss_terse: flutes — wind instruments, possibly used in temple worship
gloss_readable: This term appears in the heading of Psalm 5, in the phrase 'to the flutes' or 'for the flutes,' apparently a musical or liturgical instruction. The word's meaning is uncertain—it may derive from a root meaning 'inherit' or 'play the flute.' Ancient interpreters disagreed: some read it as referring to wind instruments, others as a melodic designation. Such superscriptions preserve liturgical terminology whose precise meanings were already obscure by late antiquity.

senses.1: A plural feminine noun in Psalm 5:1's superscription, most likely meaning 'flutes' (wind instruments), though its interpretation is disputed. The phrase 'to/for the flutes' (אֶל־הַנְּחִילוֹת) probably indicates musical accompaniment. Some connect this to חָלִיל (flute, pipe), which makes phonetic sense. Ancient versions struggled: the Greek read 'concerning the inheritance' (connecting to נַחֲלָה), while Jerome rendered 'for the inheritances.' The term likely preserves ancient musical/liturgical vocabulary.

gloss_terse: nostrils — the dual openings of the nose, especially as the source of breath and anger
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Job's description of Leviathan, the great sea creature from whose nostrils smoke streams. Hebrew typically uses the dual form for body parts that come in pairs, and nostrils naturally fit this pattern. Beyond anatomy, nostrils carry symbolic freight in Hebrew—they're the seat of anger (literally 'nose-burning') and the channel of life-breath. Here they emphasize Leviathan's terrifying, almost draconic nature.

senses.1: The dual masculine noun with possessive suffix 'his nostrils' in Job 41:20, describing how smoke comes from Leviathan's nose. The term derives from a root possibly meaning 'perforate' or related to snorting/breathing forcefully. In Job's poetic description, Leviathan's nostrils emit smoke like a boiling pot, adding to the creature's fearsome, mythic-sounding qualities. The dual form is standard for paired body parts in Hebrew.

gloss_terse: palm trees — the tall, spreading date palms characteristic of oasis landscapes
gloss_readable: In Balaam's oracle blessing Israel, he describes their tents spread out like valleys—or according to this interpretation, like palm groves. The Arabic cognate clearly means palm trees, and the image of palms spreading their fronds fits the parallel of valleys extending. Palm trees symbolized fertility, prosperity, and oasis beauty in desert regions. The text may intentionally evoke both meanings: Israel spreads like wadis and like palm plantations.

senses.1: A proposed reading in Numbers 24:6 taking כִּנְחָלִים to mean 'like palm trees' rather than 'like wadis/valleys.' Arabic نَخْل (nakhl) clearly means 'palm tree,' and the imagery of palms spreading their foliage parallels 'gardens beside a river.' Some scholars see a double meaning: Israel is like both valleys (wadis) and palm groves—both suggesting expansion and fertility. Ben Sira 50:12 may allude to this when comparing priests to 'palm branches by a wadi.'

gloss_terse: Naham — a chieftain of Judah mentioned in Chronicles' genealogies
gloss_readable: Naham appears only in 1 Chronicles among the descendants of Judah. The name means 'comfort' or 'consolation,' from the same root as Nehemiah and Nahum. Chronicles preserves many names found nowhere else, reflecting genealogical records that trace clan relationships. The Greek versions show textual variation, as is common with rare proper names.

senses.1: A personal name in 1 Chronicles 4:19, identifying a Judahite leader or clan head. The name derives from נחם (comfort, console), making it semantically related to Nahum and Nehemiah. Ancient Greek manuscripts varied in their rendering (Ναχεθ, Ναχεμ, Ναουμ), suggesting uncertainty about the exact vocalization. The genealogical context links him to the families of Judah, but beyond the name itself, Scripture provides no further information about this individual.

gloss_terse: compassion, relenting — the turning from anger to mercy, or the remorse that accompanies repentance
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Hosea's oracle where God declares, 'I will ransom them from Sheol… O Sheol, where is your compassion?' The term comes from the root meaning 'to repent, relent, be comforted.' It can indicate God's relenting from judgment or human remorse. In context, Hosea depicts God calling on Death and Sheol as instruments of judgment, demanding they show no mercy. The word captures that pivotal moment when anger might turn to compassion—which here, it doesn't.

senses.1: A masculine noun meaning 'sorrow, repentance, relenting, compassion' in Hosea 13:14. In this difficult passage, God summons death and destruction against rebellious Israel, declaring that 'compassion is hidden from my eyes'—there will be no relenting from the coming judgment. The noun derives from נחם (comfort, repent, relent), which can indicate either human remorse or divine change of intention. The rhetoric here is fierce: even Sheol is commanded to show no compassion.

gloss_terse: Nahamani — a leader among those who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and Nehemiah
gloss_readable: Nahamani appears in Nehemiah's list of returnees, bearing a name that means 'compassionate' or 'Yah has comforted.' He's among the leading men who accompanied Zerubbabel and Nehemiah back to Jerusalem. Such names were common in the exile and return period, reflecting hopes for divine comfort after judgment. The Greek version shows textual complications, possibly confusing this name with Nehemiah.

senses.1: A personal name in Nehemiah 7:7, identifying one of the leaders who returned from Babylonian captivity. The name means 'compassionate' or possibly 'Yahweh has shown compassion,' formed from נחם (comfort, console) with theophoric or adjectival ending. Ancient Greek manuscripts render this as a genitive form of Nehemiah (Νεεμιου), suggesting textual confusion or that some Greek translators identified Nahamani with Nehemiah himself. The name fits the comfort-theology common among exilic and post-exilic names.

gloss_terse: urgent, pressing — requiring immediate attention or quick action
gloss_readable: This participle describes King Saul's business when David fled to the priests at Nob. David claimed the king's matter was so urgent he had left without provisions or weapons. The word suggests pressing haste or compelling necessity. Text-critically it's uncertain, with various emendations proposed, but the sense of urgent business fits the narrative—David is fabricating an excuse for his hurried, suspicious arrival.

senses.1: A Qal passive participle functioning adjectivally, 'urgent, pressed, hurried,' in 1 Samuel 21:9 (English 21:8). David tells the priest Ahimelech that 'the king's business was urgent,' explaining why he came without proper supplies or weapons. This is part of David's deception as he flees from Saul. The Hebrew root is uncertain—possibly related to Arabic نَحَضَ (urge, press insistently). Ancient versions render with words for haste or urgency (Greek κατὰ σπουδήν). Some scholars propose reading נָאוֹץ from אוץ (press, urge).

gloss_terse: snorting — the forceful exhalation through the nostrils, especially of a horse
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Job's magnificent poem about the war horse, whose snorting is terrible. The word captures the sound and fury of a spirited stallion—nostrils flaring, breathing heavily, eager for battle. It's onomatopoetic in feel, evoking the horse's powerful presence. The term derives from a verb meaning to snort or breathe heavily, emphasizing the horse's barely-restrained energy.

senses.1: A masculine noun with possessive suffix 'its snorting' in Job 39:20, describing the terrifying sound of the war horse. Job asks rhetorically, 'Do you make him leap like a locust? His majestic snorting is terrifying.' The word emphasizes the auditory impact—the loud, forceful breathing that announces the horse's presence and intimidates enemies. It derives from a root related to heavy breathing or snorting through the nose.

gloss_terse: snorting — the sound of horses' heavy breathing, heard as a sign of approaching cavalry
gloss_readable: Jeremiah uses this feminine form to describe the sound of invading horses—their snorting heard all the way from Dan in Israel's far north. The prophet depicts the Babylonian invasion as an overwhelming cavalry force, and the sound of war horses becomes a harbinger of doom. This auditory image creates terror: before the enemy is even visible, their horses' breathing announces catastrophe. It's the same root as Job's war horse description, but in Jeremiah it signals judgment.

senses.1: A feminine construct noun 'the snorting of' in Jeremiah 8:16, describing the sound of enemy horses heard from Dan. The full phrase reads, 'From Dan is heard the snorting of his horses; at the sound of the neighing of his stallions the whole land trembles.' This is prophetic announcement of invasion—the Babylonian cavalry approaching from the north. The word shares its root with the masculine form in Job 39:20, both evoking the fierce, loud breathing of war horses. It's an aural warning of coming destruction.

gloss_terse: nakedness, lust — possibly female nakedness exposed for immoral purposes, or figuratively, shameless lust
gloss_readable: This difficult word appears in Ezekiel's extended metaphor of Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife. The context involves sexual imagery—nakedness and harlotry. While spelled like the common word for 'bronze,' the context demands a different meaning, perhaps 'lust' or 'naked shame.' The text may be corrupt, and ancient interpreters proposed various readings. The larger passage uses shocking language to depict covenant unfaithfulness as sexual betrayal.

senses.1: A disputed noun with feminine possessive suffix in Ezekiel 16:36, possibly meaning 'your nakedness' or 'your lust,' though the text is textually problematic. The verse parallels this word with 'nakedness/pudenda' (עֶרְוָה), suggesting sexual exposure or lustful behavior. The consonants match 'bronze' (נְחשֶׁת), but context requires a sexual term. Medieval Jewish commentators suggested 'lust' or 'harlotry,' while modern scholars propose various emendations (תַּזְנוּתַיִךְ 'your harlotries,' בָּשְׁתֵּךְ 'your shame'). The passage uses extreme sexual language to depict idolatry as adultery.

gloss_terse: Nehushta — the mother of King Jehoiachin, taken captive to Babylon with her son
gloss_readable: Nehushta was the queen mother when Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and deported the young king Jehoiachin. In the ancient Near East, the queen mother held significant status and influence. Her name, possibly meaning 'bronze woman' or related to the serpent, appears at a pivotal moment—2 Kings mentions her specifically when narrating the royal family's deportation. This began the final chapter of Judah's monarchy.

senses.1: A feminine personal name in 2 Kings 24:8, identifying the mother of King Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah). She was daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem and went into Babylonian exile with her son in 597 BC. The name may derive from נְחשֶׁת (bronze) or be related to נָחָשׁ (serpent). Ancient versions vary in their rendering (Greek Νεσθα, Ναισθα, Νεεσθαν). Her mention alongside Jehoiachin emphasizes the comprehensiveness of the deportation—even the queen mother was not spared.

gloss_terse: Nehushtan — the derogatory name King Hezekiah gave to the bronze serpent when he destroyed it
gloss_readable: Nehushtan was the name assigned to Moses' bronze serpent when Hezekiah destroyed it during his religious reforms. The word is likely a contemptuous pun, meaning 'mere bronze thing' or 'bronze idol.' What had been a legitimate sign of God's healing (Numbers 21) had become an object of idolatrous worship. By naming it dismissively, Hezekiah demoted it from sacred relic to mere metal. The name's exact meaning is debated—whether 'bronze god' or simply 'piece of bronze'—but the action was clear: Israel would not worship created things.

senses.1: A name given to the bronze serpent in 2 Kings 18:4 when King Hezekiah destroyed it. The object Moses had made in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9) had become an idol to which Israelites burned incense. The name is apparently pejorative, possibly meaning 'bronze thing/idol' (from נְחשֶׁת 'bronze' with nominal ending). Ancient versions varied: Greek Νεσθαλει, Νεεσθαν. Some scholars propose the name combines נָחָשׁ (serpent) + תן (a divine element), meaning 'serpent god,' which Hezekiah mockingly reduced to 'piece of bronze.' The text's wordplay on נָחָשׁ נְחשֶׁת (bronze serpent) supports the punning nature of Nehushtan.

gloss_terse: descent, lowering — the downward movement or coming down of something
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Isaiah's prophecy describing God's judgment with thunderous imagery. The phrase 'the descent of his arm' pictures God's arm coming down in a crushing blow. It's a theophanic image—divine warfare depicted in physical terms. The word emphasizes downward motion, the lowering of something from height. In context, it's part of a cluster of judgment images: thunder, flame, storm, and the arm of God descending on Assyria.

senses.1: A masculine construct noun meaning 'descent, lowering' in Isaiah 30:30, specifically 'the descent of his arm' referring to YHWH's arm coming down in judgment. The phrase pictures God's striking motion against Assyria—his arm descending in a powerful blow. The word derives from a root meaning 'go down, descend' (נחת), forming a nominal that emphasizes the downward movement. This is combined with images of divine voice, consuming fire, and tempest to create an overwhelming picture of theophanic judgment.

gloss_terse: descending, going down — moving downward, especially toward a specific location
gloss_readable: This participial adjective appears in 2 Kings during Elisha's warning to Israel's king about Aramean troop movements. The prophet reveals where the enemy is 'going down' or 'descending'—perhaps into a valley or toward a lower position for ambush. The text is textually difficult, and ancient Greek versions suggest reading 'hidden' or 'lying in wait' instead. Either way, Elisha's supernatural knowledge gives Israel tactical advantage.

senses.1: A masculine plural participle functioning adjectivally in 2 Kings 6:9, possibly meaning 'descending' or 'going down.' The phrase in context is 'Beware that you do not pass by such-and-such a place, for the Arameans are descending there.' However, the Hebrew text is uncertain—the Septuagint reads 'hidden/lying in ambush' (suggesting נֶחְבִּים from חָבָא), which many scholars prefer. The form נְחִתִּים would derive from נחת (go down, descend), describing enemy troops moving into position, possibly descending into a valley for ambush.

gloss_terse: laden with, carrying — bearing or loaded with something heavy
gloss_readable: This adjective appears in Zephaniah's judgment oracle against Jerusalem's merchant quarter. The prophet announces doom on 'those laden with silver'—the wealthy traders whose riches cannot save them. It's economic judgment: those who accumulated wealth will lose it all. The word suggests being weighed down or burdened with something, here applied to silver-carrying merchants. The image anticipates the coming catastrophe when material wealth proves worthless.

senses.1: A plural construct participial adjective meaning 'laden with, carrying, bearing' in Zephaniah 1:11. The phrase 'those laden with silver' (נְטִילֵי כָסֶף) identifies wealthy merchants or traders who will be destroyed in God's coming judgment on Jerusalem. The word suggests being loaded or burdened with weight—here, the weight of silver. The root נטל appears in later Hebrew meaning 'take up, lift, carry,' and this adjectival form describes those who carry or are laden with wealth. The judgment context indicates their riches won't save them.

gloss_terse: weight, burden — the heaviness or load of something
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Proverbs in a saying about the comparative weight of sand and stone versus a fool's provocation. The word means burden or weight, that which presses down. Paralleled with 'heaviness,' it emphasizes how physical weight is nothing compared to the exasperating burden of dealing with a fool. It's wisdom literature using concrete, measurable imagery to communicate emotional and relational reality.

senses.1: A masculine construct noun meaning 'weight, burden' in Proverbs 27:3. The verse reads, 'A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty (literally: 'and the burden of sand'), but a fool's vexation is heavier than both.' The word נֵטֶל parallels כֹּבֶד (heaviness, weight), both emphasizing physical burden. The proverb uses tactile, measurable weight to express the far greater burden of suffering a fool's provocation. The noun derives from roots related to lifting or carrying.

gloss_terse: plants, shoots — young plants or plantings, used figuratively for vigorous young men
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Psalm 144's prayer for national blessing, where sons are compared to plants grown tall in their youth. The metaphor evokes healthy agriculture—sturdy, well-established young plants representing the next generation's strength. Ancient Israel was agricultural, so such imagery naturally expressed hopes for family and national prosperity. Vigorous sons like thriving plants; fruitful daughters like carved palace pillars—these are signs of divine blessing.

senses.1: A masculine plural noun meaning 'plants, plantings' in Psalm 144:12, used figuratively. The verse prays, 'May our sons in their youth be like plants grown large,' comparing young men to well-developed plants or saplings. The imagery suggests strength, health, and promise—young plants that have grown successfully represent the vigorous next generation. This agricultural metaphor pairs with the following verse's description of daughters as carved palace corner-pillars, both images of beauty, strength, and blessing.

gloss_terse: Netaim — a location in Judah where royal potters lived and worked
gloss_readable: Netaim appears only in Chronicles, identified as a place where potters lived and worked for the king. The name likely means 'plantings' or 'planted places,' possibly indicating gardens or cultivated fields. These were royal craftsmen engaged in producing pottery—an essential industry in the ancient world. The location is otherwise unknown, preserved only in this brief genealogical note about Judahite settlements.

senses.1: A place name in 1 Chronicles 4:23, apparently a settlement in Judah where royal potters dwelt. The text describes these residents as 'potters dwelling at Netaim and Gederah; they lived there with the king for his work.' The name נְטָעִים derives from the root נטע (plant), possibly meaning 'plantings' or 'planted places/gardens.' Ancient Greek manuscripts varied in their rendering (Αζαειμ, Αταειμ, Νταειμ). The location is unidentified today, preserved only in this reference to royal potters.

gloss_terse: drops (of water) — small amounts of liquid falling or condensed
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Job's description of the water cycle, where God gathers drops of water that distill as rain. The word emphasizes smallness and plurality—individual droplets that collectively form rain. It's part of Job's sustained argument about divine wisdom in nature: God manages the minutest details of weather, gathering countless drops and transforming them into life-giving precipitation. The term captures the building blocks of meteorological phenomena.

senses.1: A masculine plural construct noun meaning 'drops of (water)' in Job 36:27. Elihu describes how God 'draws up the drops of water' (or 'gathers the water drops'), which then distill as rain from his mist. The word emphasizes the individual small droplets that constitute moisture before condensing into rain. This is part of Elihu's lengthy discourse on God's wisdom displayed in natural processes. The plural form suggests numerous tiny drops, the discrete units that aggregate into storms.

gloss_terse: stacte — an aromatic gum resin used in sacred incense, gathered as drops
gloss_readable: Stacte was one of four ingredients God commanded for the sacred incense in the tabernacle. The name relates to 'drops,' suggesting a resin that oozes or drips from plants. Its exact botanical identity is uncertain—possibilities include myrrh-related resins, storax, or balsam. Ancient versions transliterated or used 'stacte,' a Greek term for aromatic drops. The inclusion in sacred incense indicates it was precious and fragrant, part of the restricted formula for worship at God's dwelling place.

senses.1: A masculine noun in Exodus 30:34 identifying one of four ingredients for the sacred incense. God commands Moses: 'Take sweet spices—stacte, and onycha, and galbanum—sweet spices with pure frankincense.' The Hebrew נָטָף is related to 'dripping' or 'drops,' suggesting a resin collected as it exudes from plants. Exact botanical identification is uncertain: suggestions include a myrrh variety (Greek στακτή, Latin stacte), storax resin, or opobalsamum. Rabbinic tradition identified it with balsam sap. The word emphasizes the substance's liquid or semi-liquid form when harvested.

gloss_terse: keep, preserve — to guard or retain something, especially in the mind or heart
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb appears in Daniel's apocalyptic visions, where the prophet states that he kept the matter in his heart. It's the language of careful preservation—not forgetting or disclosing what was revealed. The verb is used in Aramaic portions of Scripture and related to Hebrew נָצַר (watch, guard). Daniel's response to overwhelming revelation is protective retention, holding the vision securely while pondering its meaning. Similar language appears when Mary 'treasured up' all these things in her heart.

senses.1: An Aramaic Pe'al (G-stem) perfect 1st singular verb meaning 'I kept, I preserved' in Daniel 7:28. Daniel concludes his account of the vision of four beasts: 'Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts greatly troubled me… but I kept the matter in my heart.' The verb indicates careful guarding or preserving, especially of information or memory. This is Biblical Aramaic, related to Hebrew נָצַר and Syriac נטר. The context shows Daniel holding the troubling vision privately, not immediately disclosing it.

gloss_terse: wailing, lamentation — mourning cries, especially those raised over the destroyed
gloss_readable: This term appears in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, though the text is textually uncertain. The context involves raising a funeral dirge over the fallen merchant city. The word relates to mourning and lamentation, expressing grief through vocal wailing. Ancient Near Eastern mourning practices included professional wailers who led communal expressions of grief. The text may be corrupt here—some versions read 'their sons' instead—but the overall sense is clear: Tyre will receive a lament befitting her catastrophic fall.

senses.1: A disputed masculine noun possibly meaning 'wailing, lamentation' in Ezekiel 27:32. The text reads 'they will raise over you in their wailing a lament' (or 'their sons will raise a lament'), within a sustained lament over Tyre's destruction. The word בְּנִיהֶם could be 'in their wailing' (from נְהִי/נִי = lamentation) or 'their sons' (בְּנֵיהֶם). Ancient versions divided: Greek and Syriac read 'their sons.' Many modern scholars view בְּנִיהֶם as textual corruption or gloss, preferring to omit it. If retained, it emphasizes the mourning context of this elaborate dirge.
